modelName: Ostrom Figure 2 · A framework for institutional analysis
modelNote:
Figure 2 of Ostrom's Nobel lecture (adapted from Ostrom 2005: 15). The overview of the IAD framework: three kinds of external variables shape an action situation, which generates interactions and outcomes that participants judge and that feed back. Marc's title for the whole set is kept at the top.

Lecture: Ostrom, E. (2010). Beyond Markets and States: Polycentric Governance of Complex Economic Systems. American Economic Review 100(3): 641–672 (the 2009 Nobel lecture).

Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5.5 · October 2026.

nodes.label:
Building Trust in One Another
Developing Institutional rules matched to the ecological system
nodes.note:
Marc's annotation, from his redrawing of the lecture figures. Not in Ostrom's figure.

The two halves of the lecture: trust is Figure 5; rules matched to the ecological system are Figures 4 and 6.

nodes.label: Figure 2 · A framework for institutional analysis

nodes.note: Ostrom: the broadest categories of external factors affecting an action situation at a particular time. Some of them can be self-consciously revised over time. That revision is the dashed feedback, and it is where the levels of action live (see the Levels of action drawing).

nodes.label: Biophysical Conditions
nodes.note:
Ostrom: may be simplified in some analyses to one of the four types of goods in Figure 1.

In a neighborhood: the resource itself. The water, the land, the fund, the care hours. Figure 6 unpacks this as Resource System and Resource Units.

nodes.label: Attributes of Community
nodes.note:
Ostrom: the history of prior interactions, internal homogeneity or heterogeneity of key attributes, and the knowledge and social capital of those who may participate or be affected by others.

Figure 6 unpacks this as Users. Figure 5 is about how these attributes become trust.

nodes.label: Rules-in-Use
nodes.note:
Ostrom: the common understanding of those involved about who must, must not, or may take which actions affecting others, subject to sanctions (citing Crawford and Ostrom). That definition is the Institutional Grammar.

They evolve as people interact, or are changed on purpose in a collective-choice or constitutional-choice setting.

Rules-in-use, not rules on paper. Coding a bylaw gives a first draft of this box; only observation confirms it.

nodes.label: Action Situations
nodes.note: The core of the IAD framework. Figure 3 opens it up; Figure 4 shows the rules acting on each of its parts.

nodes.label: Interactions
nodes.note: Patterns of interaction the situation generates: who takes, who contributes, who talks, who monitors, who fights.

nodes.label: Outcomes
nodes.note: What results. Ostrom: interactions and outcomes are evaluated by participants (and potentially by scholars) and feed back on both the external variables and the action situation.

nodes.label: Evaluative Criteria
nodes.note:
The yardsticks used to judge interactions and outcomes. In Ostrom 2005 these include economic efficiency, equity, accountability, conformance to values, and sustainability.

Our tools that work here: SPC charts kept over time, the protection survey, the commons viability profile.

edges.label: Judges
edges.note: 'Judges' is Marc's label, from his Figure 4 redrawing.
Outcomes feed back into the next round of the same situation.

edges.label: changes the rules
edges.note:
Added here from Ostrom's text, which says outcomes feed back on the external variables as well as the action situation. Marc's redrawing shows only the feedback to the action situation.

This arrow is where collective choice and constitutional choice live: people see the outcomes and change the rules-in-use. The Levels of action drawing opens it up.
